data.text:
**Claim 0: "A cubic yard of soil can weigh about 3,000 pounds." Supported as written.**
- OSHA's trenching transcript says "One cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a car, nearly 3,000 pounds". It adds that cave-in protection is needed for trenches more than 5 feet deep. https://www.osha.gov/vtools/construction/trench-fnl-eng-web-transcript
- Texas Department of Insurance says a single cubic yard of soil coming down on a worker weighs up to 3,000 pounds, as much as a car. https://www.tdi.texas.gov/tips/safety/trench-safety.html
- Murray State's safety office says a cubic foot can weigh as much as 114 pounds, and a cubic yard can weigh over 3,000 lb. https://www.murraystate.edu/about/Offices/esh/OccupationalSafetyHealth/TrenchingShoring/SoilTypes.aspx
- The "can weigh" and "about" wording fits. The figure is a maximum for dense or wet soil, not an average.

**Claim 1: "A 20,000-gallon pool holds about 83 tons of water." Supported, with a qualifier on the unit.**
- The sources I found were commercial water-filter sites, not government or engineering ones. My search didn't surface a USGS page.
- Science Notes says a US gallon of water weighs 8.34 lbs or 3.78 kg at 62 °F (17 °C). https://sciencenotes.org/much-gallon-water-weigh-easy-calculation/
- Epic Water Filters says a US gallon of water weighs about 8.34 pounds at room temperature. https://www.epicwaterfilters.com/blogs/quick-drips/how-much-does-water-weigh
- My arithmetic: 20,000 × 8.34 = 166,800 lb. That is about 83.4 US (short) tons of 2,000 lb, or about 75.7 metric tonnes.
- "83 tons" is therefore correct only for US short tons. The script should say "about 83 US tons (roughly 167,000 pounds)".

**Claim 2: "A typical pool pump circulates the whole pool volume through the filter about once every 8 hours." Supported in a slightly corrected form.**
- The Pool Nerd says industry standards call for at least one complete turnover every 8 hours for residential pools. https://www.thepoolnerd.com/pool-pump-size-calculator
- Clean Waves Pools says the target is to turn over the pool's full volume at least once every 8 hours. https://cleanwavespools.com/knowledgebase/pool-maintenance/pool-pump-maintenance-guide
- Swim University says a full turnover usually takes 8 to 10 hours. https://www.swimuniversity.com/run-pool-pump/
- CPO training gives an example where an eight-hour turnover means the pump and filtration system can circulate the pool's full volume in eight hours at its actual operating flow rate. https://cpo.training/pool-turnover-rate/
- Corrected form: "Residential pools are generally designed to turn over the full volume at least once about every 8 hours, and many are run 8–10 hours a day." Public and commercial pools use much shorter turnover times. These sources are mostly pool-industry sites rather than government ones.

**Claim 3: "Pool water looks blue because water absorbs red light, not because of paint." Supported in a corrected form.**
- Wikipedia's page on electromagnetic absorption by water says an absorption band at 698 nm is a 3rd overtone and tails off into the visible region. It is responsible for the intrinsic blue color of water. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_absorption_by_water
- Wikipedia's page on glacial blue ice says large quantities of liquid water are blue because of an overtone of an O–H bond stretch that absorbs light at the red end of the visible spectrum. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_ice_(glacial)
- On paint, the Waterscapes Pools article says the blue comes from a reflection of the sky or an optical illusion from pools painted blue at the bottom. These can enhance the blue hue, but neither is the reason. https://waterscapespools.com/truth-about-blue-pool-water/
- Pool-finish sources say the finish still matters. Aquabella Tile says deeper water appears more saturated because light travels farther through the water, intensifying the color effect from the finish below. https://aquabellatile.com/articles/how-pool-finishes-affect-water-color/
- Corrected form: "Water is faintly blue on its own because it absorbs red light. Pool finish and sky reflection tint or intensify that color but don't cause it." The blue comes from absorption of red light, not from scattering as in the sky. Water in a glass looks clear because the path through it is too short.
- The pool-finish and water-color sources are trade sites. The physics claim rests on the Wikipedia pages.
